title: Breaking It on Purpose: Injected Sensor Faults and the Monitor That Has to Notice Each

questions.question: Why break a simulated sensor on purpose?
options: The code that handles a real fault is the most important and least often run, since the real fault happens once a year: a simulator is the only place to run it daily
A simulated sensor never fails unless it is broken, so the monitor would otherwise never be built
Breaking it shows whether the plant model is right
A broken sensor makes the loop run faster, which exposes timing bugs
questions.explanation: Fault handling is the code that matters most when it is needed and is almost never exercised. A scenario line that breaks the sensor at a chosen time exercises it on every run.

questions.question: A stuck sensor froze at the last good reading, 2.0. What does it read when the truth is 3.0, and then 9.0?
options: 3.0 and 9.0: a stuck sensor follows the truth one sample late
2.0 and 2.0: it repeats the last good reading
0 and 0: a stuck sensor reads nothing
2.0 and 9.0: it unsticks when the truth moves far enough
questions.explanation: Stuck means frozen at the last good reading. Whatever the truth does afterwards, the sensor goes on saying 2.0.

questions.question: What is a residual?
options: The noise left after averaging several readings
The part of the command that the plant did not follow
The difference between the sensor and what a model says it should read, near zero when all is well
The alarm threshold less the current reading
questions.explanation: A copy of the plant model is driven by the same commands, and the sensor is compared with it. A lying sensor shows up as a gap between the two.

questions.question: A spike of 0.4 on one reading in 25 was never caught by a monitor needing three in a row. Why is that not a bug?
options: It is a bug: a monitor should catch every bad reading
One reading is not a run: the monitor was built to ignore a single reading, and whether a lone spike matters is for a different monitor, such as a Hampel filter
The spike was smaller than the threshold of 0.02
The spike fell between two samples and was never read
questions.explanation: Asking for three in a row is what stops one noisy sample from raising an alarm. The same rule lets a one sample spike through, which is a job for another kind of filter.

questions.question: A stuck sensor at the target was caught by the residual monitor 2.85 s late and by the stuck monitor at the move. Why?
options: The residual threshold was too high, and the stuck monitor has none
The shadow model was 2.85 s behind the plant
The stuck monitor runs faster than the residual monitor
A frozen reading at the target looks right and the loop commands almost nothing, so the residual stays small; the stuck monitor knows an unchanging reading is wrong only when motion was expected
questions.explanation: Frozen at about the right value, the sensor and the shadow agree. Only when the robot was told to move did an unchanging reading become evidence.

questions.question: What did raising the residual threshold from 0.02 to 0.2 cost, against a drift of 0.05 a second?
options: Nothing: a higher threshold only removes false alarms
The drift was not found at all
The drift was found 4.04 s after it began instead of 0.46: nine times later, with the position by then wrong by 0.2
The drift was found twice as late, at 0.92 s
questions.explanation: Too low and healthy runs raise alarms: 200 of 200 at twice the noise. Too high and a real drift runs on for seconds. Both costs can be read from the simulation.
